<reason>Both sides argued well within the rules, but CON built a more disciplined, cumulative case around a single structural asymmetry — that a pure ban permanently forecloses any lever (fees, set-asides) to fund the sewer/school/street capacity that growth eventually requires — and pressed it consistently from opening through closing, culminating in the sharp "cannot be both harmless and transformative" dilemma. PRO's counter (that broad legalization eventually funds infrastructure via a larger tax base) is a reasonable idea but remained underdeveloped and asserted rather than mechanistically defended, leaving CON's pressure question on windfall recapture only partially answered. PRO's strongest thread — that bonus programs can be quietly killed by administrative "screw-tightening" without a vote, while a ban creates a broad, hard-to-reverse constituency — was a good counter to CON's political-fragility argument, but CON neutralized much of its force by noting that councils can just as easily re-impose parking minimums or design review after a ban, making durability roughly symmetric rather than a clear PRO advantage. Both used the Q&A format correctly and answered pointedly, but CON's questions exposed a genuine unresolved tension in PRO's case (growth must be simultaneously slow enough to be harmless and large enough to matter) that PRO never fully dissolved, giving CON the cleaner, more decisive throughline by the closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.5] dilemma — "PRO's case depends on growth being big enough to matter but never big enough to need paying for" — built on the Pressure Questions exchange, was the most decisive moment; PRO's [A4.3] answer (broad legalization "grows the tax base") gestured at a response but never concretely rebutted the targeted-funding critique.</best_rebuttal>
